*Days without rain: 119. Buckets from the spring: 7.*

The stars over Black Pool were too close. They hung low enough that Mei felt she could reach up and knock on one, and there were so many of them that the sky looked like a spilled jar of glass beads. The wind had died. The mist curled around the dragon’s sea-green flank, a soft, damp blanket that smelled of clean stone and old rain.

Tao was asleep, snoring softly into his yellow rain boots. He had fallen asleep mid-sentence, asking if dragons dig their noses. Hua lay on her side, one hand clamped tight over her notebook, as if it contained the answers to a test she had forgotten to take. Mei sat up, her back against the rough, warm scales. Yun did not sleep. Dragons, he explained quietly, did not need it as much. He kept his amber eyes wide, watching the dark water.

Mei pressed her thumb into her palm. The cold stone bit back. She looked at the pearl under his chin. It was not bright. It was a dull, tired grey, heavy with all the unshed rain.

"It is a good night for thinking," Yun said, his voice a low rumble that she felt in her ribs.

"Or for hiding," she whispered.

He turned his head. "Hiding is safer. But the rain is waiting."

pages.text:
Mei picked at a loose thread on her sleeve while the silence grew thick enough to chew. It was the kind of quiet that made her ears ring, like a school bell that someone had forgotten to stop. She wanted to say something to break it, but the words stuck in her throat, just like they always did.

"In class," she started, then stopped to look at her hands. "When Teacher Luo asks a question, my mind goes white. It is not that I do not know the answer. It is that I cannot hear my own voice."

Yun did not say "oh" or "that is nice." He just listened, the way the still water listened to the stones beneath it, without asking for anything in return.

"And then I go home," she continued, her voice dropping to a whisper. "And I think about the calls with Mama and Baba. They say we are fine. But it is not fine. It is dry. And I am small."

"But you said 'I will go,'" Yun said gently. "In front of the whole village."

Mei shrugged, her shoulders rising and falling in a slow, tired rhythm. "It came out like a leaf. Barely there."

Yun’s whiskers twitched. "Then it was a leaf that crossed a mountain."

pages.text:
Mei thought about Nainai’s bamboo stick, that tiny fence of absence where each notch marked a dry morning. She pictured the seedlings in the terraces, yellow and brittle, waiting for a signal they could not give themselves.

"In the old stories," she said, "when the Awakening of Insects comes, the thunder wakes them up. The ants. The frogs. The seeds in the ground. They are sleeping. They are cold."

She looked up at the dragon. "Thunder is not just a loud noise, Yun. It is a knock. It is a knock on the door of spring."

Yun went very still, and the mist around his shoulders stopped swirling. His amber eyes grew wide. He looked at the dark, dry ground, then back at Mei.

"A knock?" he repeated. The word seemed to surprise him. "I have always thought of it as a warning. A shout. Something to make them run."

"No," Mei said, surprised by the steady strength in her own voice. "It is an invitation. To wake up."

pages.text:
Yun’s whiskers trembled, and he looked down at his own slender claws, then at the heavy, grey pearl resting under his chin. For a hundred years, he had hidden. He had tucked himself behind rocks and wrapped himself in mist, so busy being afraid of the noise he made that he had never stopped to listen to what it did.

"I have never seen what happens after," he whispered. "I hid too fast. I never saw the frogs jump. I never saw the green come up the terraces. I only saw the fear."

He let out a long, shuddering breath that fogged the cool air.

"I thought I was a noise that frightened people," he said slowly. "I did not know I was a knock."

Mei reached out and touched one of his soft, branching antlers. It was warm, and it was alive. She did not say "it will be okay," because she knew it might not be. But she stayed. She breathed in for four, held for one, and breathed out for four, feeling the steady rhythm settle in her chest like a drumbeat in a quiet room.

pages.text:
The night air was crisp. The stars still hung low, watching. Mei and Yun looked at each other. No words were needed, not yet. They were children, in a way. Making a promise in the dark, where it felt safer.

Mei took a breath. "I will say the words," she said. "When it matters. I will say them aloud, for everyone to hear."

Yun nodded. His amber eyes were bright, not with water, but with light. "And I will make a thunder," he said. "A real one. When the time comes."

They did not say they were not afraid. They did not promise it would be easy. The pearl under his chin glowed a little brighter, a soft, hopeful silver. Above them, a single, small cloud drifted across the stars, moving slowly, like a ship on a dark sea.
